Daytona’s `Sandbox` exposes `RefreshData`, `Start`, `Stop`, `Pause`, `Archive`, and `Delete` on every sandbox. `Pause` and `Archive` post to the API with the sandbox ID. The SDK does not look at the sandbox class or `gpu_count` before that call. `Stop` is documented as preserving state. Modal’s `Sandbox` exposes `Terminate`. It has no start, stop, pause, archive, or delete method. `FromID` does not look the sandbox up, which is why Kit’s `Attach` is the right Modal call.

So the lists should be static:

| Provider | `Capabilities` |
| --- | --- |
| Daytona | `Refresh`, `Start`, `Stop`, `Pause`, `Archive`, `Delete` |
| Modal | `Terminate` |

A missing method stays `ErrorKindUnsupported`, returned in the SDK with no provider request. That is what `Pause` on a Modal handle does today.

Class and GPU acceptance belong to Daytona’s API. Kit should call `Pause` or `Archive` and map the error Daytona returns. The local checks in `PauseSandbox` and `ArchiveSandbox` already fetch the sandbox and then reject it, so a container whose list omits `Pause` still pays for a Daytona `Get`. The list does not prevent that call.

Keep two lightweight handle checks, separate from capabilities. A closed handle and a handle that has already completed `Terminate` or `Delete` return `ErrorKindFailedPrecondition` and do not call the provider. Those checks are “this handle cannot make another call,” not “the provider lacks the method.”

The cache, the `SandboxInfo` clone, and the GPU and class walk in `Capabilities` can go. They duplicate a policy the pinned SDKs do not implement, and the lifecycle methods do not read the result.

## What this pull request does

Go and TypeScript get the same two changes.

The copy reductions keep the same results. `Info()` / `info()` still returns its own copy, so a caller cannot change the handle by editing that result. `Close` / `close()` still releases only the local handle. It does not stop or delete the cloud sandbox.

`Capabilities` / `capabilities()` and `Supports` / `supports()` now list the lifecycle methods that provider implements. A live Daytona handle lists refresh, start, stop, pause, archive, and delete. A live Modal handle lists terminate. Class and GPU stay on the sandbox metadata. Daytona accepts or rejects pause, archive, and stop for that sandbox, and Kit returns that error.

## 1. A lifecycle call reads a few flags

Start, stop, pause, and the other lifecycle calls need the sandbox id, whether this handle is closed, and whether the sandbox is already finished.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Start] --> B[Read the id, closed, and terminal]
```

Example. The handle stores this record:

```text
id:        sb-123
state:     running
terminal:  false
metadata:  a large map of labels and provider fields
```

`Start` reads `sb-123`, `closed = false`, and `terminal = false`, and leaves the stored record where it is.

An empty id still fails before a closed handle does. Both still return "sandbox handle is not initialized" or "sandbox handle is closed".

## 2. The id sent to the provider is the id when the call runs

Only one lifecycle call runs at a time. The others wait at a gate. While a call is waiting, another call can replace the sandbox record, including the id.

The id is read after this call gets through the gate. The provider then sees that id.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Stop
  participant Gate
  participant Refresh
  participant Provider
  Stop->>Gate: wait
  Refresh->>Provider: refresh sb-123
  Provider-->>Refresh: sandbox is now sb-456
  Gate-->>Stop: your turn
  Stop->>Provider: stop sb-456
```

Closed and terminal are checked again after the gate, in the same order as before. A call that was already waiting cannot start after `Close` has finished.

## 3. Capabilities list the provider's methods

Go checks which lifecycle interfaces the backend implements. TypeScript checks which methods are present on the backend. The list is computed from that. It is not saved, and it does not read the sandbox class or `gpu_count`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Q[Capabilities] --> L{Closed or terminal}
  L -->|yes| N[Return nothing]
  L -->|no| P[List the provider methods]
```

| Provider | Live handle |
| --- | --- |
| Daytona | refresh, start, stop, pause, archive, delete |
| Modal | terminate |

A closed client, a closed handle, or a terminal sandbox returns nothing. After `Terminate` or `Delete`, a later lifecycle call fails with `ErrorKindFailedPrecondition` ("sandbox lifecycle is terminal") and does not call the provider. A method the provider never implemented fails with `ErrorKindUnsupported` before a provider call.

Example. A Daytona container with a GPU still lists pause and archive. `Pause` calls Daytona. Daytona accepts or rejects that sandbox, and the SDK returns that error. A Modal handle lists terminate. `Pause` on that handle fails with `ErrorKindUnsupported` and does not call Modal.

## 4. Daytona writes provider metadata directly

When Daytona returns a sandbox, the SDK already has plain values: a GPU count, a few strings, a boolean, and four interval numbers. Those values are written straight into metadata fields. Optional strings go through one writer in each language, and the four intervals go through one number writer. A missing string is left out.

```text
gpu_count = 2
snapshot = base
auto_stop_interval_minutes = 0
auto_pause_interval_minutes = 0
auto_archive_interval_minutes = 0
auto_delete_interval_minutes = 0
```

`gpu_count` is included only when the count is greater than zero. `spot` is included only when it is true. A zero interval is still stored, because Daytona always reports those four intervals.

## 5. User metadata is checked and stored in one walk

`MetadataObjectFromMap` / `metadataObjectFromMap` is the path for metadata an application supplies. It still rejects a map that is too deep, has too many nodes, has too much text, or contains a value that is not a finite number. It checks the limits and builds the values in the same walk. Byte slices are still copied once, so the caller can reuse their own slice.

The error text is unchanged: "exceeds maximum depth or contains a cycle", "exceeds node budget", "exceeds byte budget", "requires finite numbers", and "unsupported metadata value type".

## 6. Lifecycle options copy only the fields the provider needs

Start, stop, pause, archive, terminate, and delete share one timeout rule. When no timeout is recorded, the caller message is passed through. When a timeout is recorded, that operation builds a new message and fills its own fields. Stop copies `force`, and terminate and delete copy `wait`, only when the caller set them.

```text
StopOptions{ Timeout: 5s, Force: true }
```

The provider receives a new message with that timeout and `force = true`. The caller's message is not edited. An unset `force` stays unset. Unset means "use the provider default", and `false` means "do not force". An explicit zero timeout still overrides the client timeout.

## 7. TypeScript copies a create request only where a duration sits

Create requests use millisecond numbers in `timeout`, `queueTimeout`, `maximumLifetime`, and `after`. Validation turns those numbers into protobuf durations. An object is copied only when one of those fields is inside it. Labels and other plain data stay as the caller wrote them.

```text
{
  snapshot: "base",
  timeout: 30000,
  labels: { team: "platform" }
}
```

`timeout` becomes a protobuf duration. `snapshot` and `labels` are not copied. Validation does not change the caller's object.

Lifecycle requests in TypeScript are flat `{ timeout?, force?, wait? }`. Those are copied with a shallow copy. `info()` still uses a deep copy.

## Changes in TypeScript and Go

Both SDKs do the same work. The TypeScript details below are what `0.1.4` ships. The Go details are in https://github.com/sandbox-kit/kit/issues/31.

### A lifecycle call reads a few flags

Start, stop, pause, and the other lifecycle calls need the sandbox id, whether the handle is closed, and whether the sandbox is terminal.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Start] --> B[Read the id, closed, and terminal]
```

Example. The handle stores `id: sb-123`, `terminal: false`, and a large metadata map. `Start` reads those three facts and leaves the stored record where it is. An empty id still fails before a closed handle does.

The id sent to the provider is the id on the handle when that call is allowed to run. If refresh changes `sb-123` to `sb-456` while stop is waiting, stop sends `sb-456`.

### Capabilities list the provider's methods

`capabilities()` lists the lifecycle methods present on the backend. A live Daytona handle lists refresh, start, stop, pause, archive, and delete. A live Modal handle lists terminate. Class and GPU stay on the metadata. They do not change this list.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Q[capabilities] --> L{Closed or terminal}
  L -->|yes| N[Return nothing]
  L -->|no| P[List the provider methods]
```

A closed handle or a terminal sandbox returns nothing. After `terminate` or `delete`, a later lifecycle call fails with `ErrorKindFailedPrecondition` and does not call the provider. A method the provider never implemented throws `ErrorKindUnsupported` before a provider call.

`pause` and `archive` call Daytona. Daytona accepts or rejects that sandbox, and Kit returns that error. Modal's provider no longer supplies its own capability list. The sandbox package sees `terminate` and lists terminate.

Go builds the same list from the backend interfaces. That ships in sandbox and Daytona `v0.1.2`. The Go Modal provider is unchanged and stays at `v0.1.1`.

### Daytona writes metadata directly

Provider metadata is built from the values Daytona just returned. Optional strings and the four interval numbers each go through one writer. `gpu_count` is stored only when it is greater than zero. `spot` is stored only when it is true. A zero interval is still stored.

```text

snapshot = base
auto_stop_interval_minutes = 0
auto_pause_interval_minutes = 0
auto_archive_interval_minutes = 0
auto_delete_interval_minutes = 0
```

### User metadata is checked and stored in one walk

`metadataObjectFromMap` still rejects a map that is too deep, has too many nodes, has too much text, or contains a non-finite number. It checks those limits and builds the values in the same walk.

### Lifecycle options and duration fields

A lifecycle request is a flat `{ timeout?, force?, wait? }`. The provider receives a shallow copy. `info()` still returns a deep copy.

Create validation turns `timeout`, `queueTimeout`, `maximumLifetime`, and `after` from milliseconds into protobuf durations. An object is copied only when one of those fields is inside it. `labels` and other plain data stay as the caller wrote them.

```text
{
  snapshot: "base",
  timeout: 30000,
  labels: { team: "platform" }
}
```

`timeout` becomes a protobuf duration. `snapshot` and `labels` are not copied. Validation does not change the caller's object.

**`Client.Close` already matches both SDKs.** Nothing to change there.

Daytona `Client.Close` and `[Symbol.asyncDispose]` shut down the event subscription and dispatcher, then flush OpenTelemetry. Modal `Client.Close` closes the gRPC connections. Kit calls those. Neither call stops or deletes the cloud sandbox.

**`Sandbox.Close` has no matching call on either SDK for the way Kit holds a sandbox.**

Daytona’s `Sandbox` type has no close or dispose method. Handle close correctly does nothing.

Modal’s `Sandbox.Detach` only disconnects that one local object. It closes that object’s command-router connection and leaves the cloud sandbox running. Kit does not keep the object from create, attach, or terminate. Each call builds one, uses it, and drops it.

TypeScript handle close still does `sandboxes.fromId(id).detach()`. `fromId` only constructs a new object, and `detach` then flips the flag on that new object. The object from create or terminate is already gone, so this does not release a connection Kit is holding. Go does not call `Detach`, which matches that usage.
